title: WebSockets, SSE, gRPC and proxies
scopeHtml:
Scope: real-time protocols, gRPC, and proxies and load balancers at the protocol level.

Scope: real-time protocols, gRPC, and proxies and load balancers at the protocol level.

notes.title: Why plain request/response is not enough
notes.html:
HTTP request/response only lets the client speak first. Real-time features (chat, live scores, notifications, collaborative editing) need the server to push data the moment it exists.

Options, from simplest to most powerful:

  1. Polling: client asks every N seconds. Simple, wasteful: 1M users polling every 5 s = 200,000 requests/s, mostly "nothing new".
  2. Long polling: client asks, server holds the request open until there is data (or 30 s), client immediately asks again. Works everywhere, one connection per user, a request cycle per message.
  3. Server-Sent Events (SSE): one long-lived HTTP response; server streams events down.
  4. WebSocket: one upgraded connection, both sides send freely.
  5. gRPC streaming: typed streams over HTTP/2, mainly service to service.

Worked example. 100,000 users, a notification arrives on average once an hour. Polling every 10 s: 10,000 requests/s that return nothing. SSE or WebSocket: 100,000 idle connections (about 10 to 50 KB RAM each, so 1 to 5 GB) and about 28 messages/s. Connections are cheap on modern event-loop servers (Netty, Node, Go, Nginx), polling is expensive in requests.

Industry examples. Slack, WhatsApp Web and Discord use WebSockets. Firebase and Android FCM use persistent connections. Twitter used long polling and SSE-like streams historically.

Everyday analogy. Checking the letterbox every five minutes (polling) versus a doorbell that rings when the postman arrives (push).

Common interview traps.

  • Saying WebSockets are always better. If you only need server-to-client, SSE is simpler and plays well with proxies and auto-reconnect.
  • Not counting the connection cost: file descriptors, memory, load balancer limits.

notes.title: WebSockets
notes.html:
A WebSocket starts as an HTTP request that asks to be upgraded into a persistent, full-duplex TCP connection carrying small framed messages. After the upgrade, no more HTTP headers per message: just 2 to 14 bytes of framing.

Handshake:

GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: ws.shop.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

Details seniors know:

  • Frames: text, binary, ping, pong, close. Ping/pong every 20 to 30 s keeps NATs and proxies from dropping idle connections (many close at 60 s idle).
  • Client frames are masked (stops cache-poisoning of intermediaries).
  • No automatic reconnect, no delivery guarantee, no ordering across reconnects. You must add message IDs, acks and resume tokens.
  • Stateful: the connection lives on one server. To message user B you must find B's server: a Redis pub/sub or a presence map.
  • Auth: browsers cannot set custom headers on new WebSocket(), so use a cookie, or a short-lived token in the query string or first message.

Config (nginx).

# location /ws/ {
#   proxy_pass http://ws_backend;
#   proxy_http_version 1.1;
#   proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
#   proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
#   proxy_read_timeout 3600s;   # default 60s kills idle sockets
# }

Worked example. One 8 GB server with 30 KB per connection holds ~250,000 sockets (check ulimit -n, ephemeral ports on the LB side, and kernel somaxconn). WhatsApp famously reached 2M connections on one box (Erlang, FreeBSD, tuned). For 5M users online you need ~20 servers at 250k each plus headroom.

Decision gravity. Choosing WebSocket makes your service stateful: deploys must drain connections gracefully and clients must handle reconnect storms (thundering herd after a deploy: use jittered backoff). Reversible only with effort, since clients are shipped.

Everyday analogy. A phone call: the line stays open and either side talks whenever, but you must handle dropped calls yourself.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting heartbeat and proxy idle timeouts (AWS ALB idle default 60 s).
  • Round-robin LB leaves connection counts uneven after a restart (all clients reconnect to the first healthy node).
  • Assuming messages are never lost; design for at-least-once with ids.

notes.title: Server-Sent Events (SSE)
notes.html:
SSE is a long-lived text/event-stream HTTP response where the server writes events and the browser's EventSource delivers them, reconnecting automatically.

GET /stream HTTP/1.1
Accept: text/event-stream

HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Cache-Control: no-cache

id: 41
event: price
data: {"sym":"INFY","px":1523.4}

id: 42
data: {"sym":"TCS","px":3911.0}

Strengths:

  • Plain HTTP: works through proxies, CDNs that allow streaming, HTTP/2 multiplexing.
  • Built-in resume: after a drop the browser reconnects and sends Last-Event-ID: 42, so the server can replay.
  • Tiny API. Perfect for dashboards, notifications, log tail, and LLM token streaming (ChatGPT-style APIs use it).

Limits: one direction only (client uses ordinary POSTs); text only (base64 for binary); on HTTP/1.1, browsers allow only ~6 connections per host across all tabs (HTTP/2 raises this to ~100 streams).

Worked example. Live cricket score: 2M viewers, an update every 5 s, ~300 bytes each. Fan-out = 2M x 300 B / 5 s = 120 MB/s = ~1 Gbit/s, which is why you put a CDN/edge layer that fans out one stream per region, as Hotstar-style systems do, rather than origin connections.

Decision gravity. SSE is the lowest-regret choice for server-to-client updates (easy to swap for WebSocket later because the event format is yours). Compression and proxy buffering can silently delay events: set X-Accel-Buffering: no for nginx and disable gzip on the stream.

Everyday analogy. A radio broadcast with a tape you can rewind to a numbered marker after the signal drops.

Common interview traps.

  • Proxies buffering the stream, so events arrive in bursts.
  • No keep-alive comment lines (: ping) so idle proxies drop the stream.
  • Using SSE where the client must also send low-latency messages (games, collaborative editing).

notes.title: gRPC
notes.html:
gRPC is a framework for calling remote functions: you describe services and messages in a .proto file, tools generate client and server code, and calls travel as Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2.

service OrderService {
  rpc GetOrder (GetOrderRequest) returns (Order);              // unary
  rpc WatchOrders (Filter) returns (stream Order);             // server streaming
  rpc Upload (stream Chunk) returns (Summary);                 // client streaming
  rpc Chat (stream Msg) returns (stream Msg);                  // bidirectional
}

Why teams adopt it:

  • Binary protobuf: typically 3x to 10x smaller than JSON and faster to parse; schema evolution via field numbers (never reuse a number).
  • HTTP/2: multiplexing, streaming, header compression, flow control.
  • Deadlines and cancellation propagate across services, status codes (OK, UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED) are standard.
  • Codegen in Java, Kotlin, Go, Swift: no hand-written clients.

Limits:

  • Browsers cannot speak raw gRPC (no control over HTTP/2 framing/trailers) so use gRPC-Web via a proxy such as Envoy.
  • Harder to debug by eye (binary): use grpcurl, reflection, Wireshark with the proto.
  • Load balancing pitfall: one long-lived HTTP/2 connection means an L4 balancer pins all calls from a client to one backend. Use L7 balancing (Envoy, Linkerd) or client-side balancing with a resolver.

Worked example. A 1 KB JSON order is ~350 bytes in protobuf. At 20,000 internal calls/s that is 13 MB/s versus 20 MB/s, and often 30 to 50% less CPU for (de)serialisation. Set a deadline of 300 ms at the edge and every hop sees the remaining time.

Industry examples. Google (origin as Stubby), Netflix, Square, Uber and Dropbox use gRPC internally; Kubernetes' etcd and many CNCF projects speak it. Android's OkHttp-based grpc-okhttp is common in mobile.

Decision gravity. Choosing protobuf as the internal contract is hard to reverse across many services, but the evolution rules (add optional fields, never renumber) make it safe. Public APIs usually stay REST/JSON, optionally with gRPC-JSON transcoding.

Everyday analogy. A company with an internal phone directory and a strict form for each request, far quicker than writing a free-form letter.

Common interview traps.

  • L4 load balancing pinning gRPC traffic.
  • No deadlines, so a slow dependency piles up threads.
  • Retrying non-idempotent RPCs; enable retries only with a retry policy and idempotency.

notes.title: Proxies and load balancers at the protocol level
notes.html:
A forward proxy acts for clients (corporate egress filtering); a reverse proxy acts for servers (hides them, terminates TLS, balances load, caches). Load balancers are reverse proxies with a pool.

Layers:

  • L4 (TCP/UDP): sees IP and port only; forwards bytes; no TLS termination (or passthrough). Very fast, millions of connections. Examples: AWS NLB, HAProxy tcp mode, LVS/IPVS, Katran, Maglev.
  • L7 (HTTP/gRPC): parses requests, so it can route by path/host/header, retry, rate-limit, rewrite, terminate TLS, cache and speak h2 to clients and h1 upstream. Examples: AWS ALB, NGINX, Envoy, HAProxy http mode.
  • Direct Server Return (DSR): the LB handles only inbound packets; the server replies straight to the client. Great for asymmetric traffic (video).

Protocol-level things that bite:

  • Connection pooling to upstreams: many client connections multiplex into few upstream connections.
  • Timeouts: client idle, upstream connect, upstream read. Mismatch = random 502/504.
  • Retries: only for idempotent requests or failures before the request was sent; or retry storms double the load.
  • Proxy protocol / X-Forwarded-For: how the app learns the real client IP.
  • Health checks: active (probe) and passive (outlier detection by consecutive 5xx).
  • Algorithms: round robin, least connections, least request (Envoy "least request" with power of two choices), consistent hashing, locality-aware.

Config (Envoy-style idea, nginx syntax).

# upstream api { least_conn; server 10.0.1.10:8080 max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s;
#                server 10.0.1.11:8080; keepalive 64; }
# proxy_connect_timeout 1s; proxy_read_timeout 15s;
# proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502;   # retry only safe cases

Worked example (the classic 502). ALB idle timeout 60 s; app closes keep-alive after 5 s. ALB sends a request on a connection the app just closed, resets it, user sees 502. Fix: app keep-alive timeout greater than the LB idle timeout (e.g. 75 s vs 60 s).

Industry examples. Cloudflare, Fastly at the edge; Envoy as the service-mesh sidecar (Istio, Lyft); Netflix Zuul gateway; Facebook Katran for L4.

Decision gravity. Where you terminate TLS is a key choice: at the edge (simple, cleartext inside) or end to end with mTLS (more secure, more cert management). Switching later touches every service.

Everyday analogy. A receptionist (L7) reads your visit reason and directs you; a turnstile (L4) just counts people and lets them through.

Common interview traps.

  • Mismatched timeouts across layers.
  • Blind retries on POST.
  • Forgetting the LB is itself a SPOF; use active-passive pairs, anycast or DNS.

notes.title: Choosing between them
notes.html:
Need Pick Why
Server to browser feed SSE Simple, auto-resume
Chat, games, two-way WebSocket Low overhead both ways
Service to service, typed gRPC Contracts, deadlines, speed
Public simple API REST over HTTP Universal, cacheable
Rare updates Polling or push notification Cheapest

Worked example. A trading dashboard: price ticks to browsers use SSE through a CDN; order placement uses REST POST; internal matching services use gRPC; a mobile chat tab uses WebSocket. Mixed is normal.

Common interview traps.

  • Picking one protocol for everything.
  • Ignoring that mobile OSes kill background sockets; use FCM/APNs push for wake-up.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Polling is wasteful, long polling is a compatible fallback; SSE and WebSocket are the real push options.
  • WebSocket: HTTP upgrade (101), framed, stateful; needs heartbeats, resume ids, and broker fan-out across servers.
  • SSE: one-way over HTTP, built-in reconnect with Last-Event-ID; watch for proxy buffering.
  • gRPC: protobuf over HTTP/2, streaming, deadlines; needs L7 or client-side balancing; browsers need gRPC-Web.
  • L4 proxies forward bytes; L7 proxies understand HTTP, route, retry, terminate TLS; align timeouts and retry only safe requests.
  • Match protocol to need; stateful connections require graceful drains and jittered reconnect.

questions.promptHtml: HTTP is request/response. How do you get data from server to client the moment it exists, and what are your options?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you can reason about cost (requests, connections, memory) instead of naming WebSocket by reflex.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: HTTP lets only the client speak first, so I have four options. Polling asks every N seconds: simple but wasteful. Long polling holds the request open until data exists: works everywhere, but a request cycle per message. SSE is one long-lived response streaming events down: one-way, auto-reconnect. WebSocket is an upgraded two-way connection. I pick by direction and by what the proxies in the path allow.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Cost model, 100,000 users, one notification per user per hour:

Polling every 10 s : 100,000 / 10 = 10,000 req/s, almost all "nothing new"
Long polling       : ~100,000 held requests + ~28 msg/s re-issues
SSE / WebSocket    : 100,000 idle sockets (10-50 KB each = 1-5 GB RAM) + ~28 msg/s

Polling costs requests; push costs held connections. Event-loop servers (Netty, Nginx, Node, Go) hold idle sockets cheaply, so push usually wins above a few thousand users. The real costs of push are file descriptors, memory, LB connection limits, and graceful draining on deploy.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "WebSocket is always better": if only server to client is needed, SSE is simpler and survives proxies better.
  • Ignoring connection cost (fds, RAM, LB limits).
  • Polling for rare events at high frequency instead of a mobile push (FCM/APNs).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When is polling the right answer? -> Rare updates, tolerant of 30-60 s delay, tiny user count; zero infra change.
  2. Why does long polling still exist? -> It works through any proxy and old browsers; it is the fallback in Socket.IO-style libraries.
  3. How does mobile change this? -> OSes kill background sockets, so use FCM/APNs to wake the app, then fetch over HTTP.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the four names. Senior computes req/s versus held connections, names the failure mode of each (buffering proxies, idle timeouts, reconnect storms) and picks the cheapest that meets the direction requirement.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team polled every 3 s from 400k mobile clients (133k req/s of empty responses) and spent more on API pods than on the feature was worth; moving to SSE plus push notifications cut API load by 90%.

questions.promptHtml: How does a WebSocket connection get established, and what is different on the wire afterwards?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you know WebSocket is an HTTP upgrade and not a separate port or protocol family, which explains proxy behavior.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The client sends a normal HTTP/1.1 GET with Upgrade: websocket and a random Sec-WebSocket-Key. If the server agrees it answers 101 Switching Protocols with Sec-WebSocket-Accept, a hash of that key. From then on the same TCP connection carries small framed messages in both directions, 2 to 14 bytes of overhead instead of HTTP headers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
GET /chat HTTP/1.1
Host: ws.shop.com
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

The Accept value proves the server understood the upgrade (it is not security). Frame types: text, binary, ping, pong, close. Client-to-server frames are masked so a buggy intermediary cannot be tricked into cache poisoning. The connection is now stateful and lives on exactly one server. Auth: browsers cannot set custom headers on new WebSocket(), so use the cookie sent in the handshake, or a short-lived token in the query string or first message.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking Accept authenticates the client.
  • No ping/pong: NATs and proxies drop idle connections at about 60 s.
  • Long-lived JWT in the URL (lands in access logs); use a one-time ticket.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why mask client frames? -> Stops attackers crafting bytes that a caching proxy mistakes for HTTP responses.
  2. Does WebSocket guarantee delivery after a reconnect? -> No; add message ids, acks, resume tokens.
  3. What changes for HTTP/2? -> RFC 8441 tunnels WebSocket over an h2 stream (extended CONNECT); support varies, verify on your proxy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "upgrade handshake, full duplex". Senior adds masking, no built-in reconnect or ordering across reconnects, statefulness, and the auth-on-handshake constraint.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A chat service put the JWT in the query string; it showed up in ALB access logs and a vendor's log pipeline. They moved to a 30 s single-use ticket.

questions.promptHtml: What is Server-Sent Events, and how does it recover after a dropped connection?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: SSE is the underrated tool for one-way feeds; the interviewer checks you know its built-in reconnect and its limits.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SSE is one long-lived HTTP response with Content-Type: text/event-stream; the server writes id:, event: and data: lines and the browser's EventSource parses them. On a drop, the browser reconnects automatically and sends Last-Event-ID, so the server can replay what was missed. It is one-way and text-only.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/event-stream
Cache-Control: no-cache

id: 41
event: price
data: {"sym":"INFY","px":1523.4}

id: 42
data: {"sym":"TCS","px":3911.0}

Reconnect request carries Last-Event-ID: 42; the server resumes from 43, which requires a replay buffer (Redis stream, Kafka offset) keyed by that id. Limits: HTTP/1.1 browsers allow about 6 connections per host across tabs (HTTP/2 raises this to roughly 100 streams); binary needs base64. Send a : ping comment every 15-25 s so idle proxies keep the stream.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Not storing ids, so "auto-resume" silently loses events.
  • gzip or proxy buffering delaying events.
  • Using SSE for client-to-server low-latency traffic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you send data client to server? -> Ordinary POST/fetch alongside the stream.
  2. How do you set auth headers? -> Native EventSource cannot; use cookies or a fetch-based SSE polyfill.
  3. How would LLM token streaming use it? -> POST with fetch, read the text/event-stream body incrementally; ids matter less.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "one-way push". Senior adds Last-Event-ID plus a replay store, the 6-connection HTTP/1.1 limit, and the buffering gotchas.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A dashboard on SSE lost 30 s of events on every deploy until ids were backed by a Redis stream with 5 minutes of retention.

questions.promptHtml: What is gRPC actually built on, and why can a browser not call it directly?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates people who use generated stubs from those who understand what runs underneath (HTTP/2, trailers, framing).

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: gRPC is Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2. You define services in a .proto, codegen makes clients and servers, and each call is an HTTP/2 stream with a length-prefixed protobuf message, with the status sent in trailers. Browsers cannot control HTTP/2 framing or read trailers, so they use gRPC-Web through a proxy such as Envoy.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Request : HEADERS(:path=/shop.OrderService/GetOrder, content-type: application/grpc, grpc-timeout: 300m)
          DATA( [1B compressed flag][4B length][protobuf bytes] )
Response: HEADERS(:status 200)  DATA(...)  TRAILERS(grpc-status: 0, grpc-message)

Four shapes: unary, server stream, client stream, bidi. Benefits: multiplexing many calls on one connection, HPACK header compression, flow control, deadlines that propagate (grpc-timeout), standard status codes (UNAVAILABLE, DEADLINE_EXCEEDED). Schema evolution: add fields with new numbers; never reuse or renumber a field.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
service OrderService {
  rpc GetOrder (GetOrderRequest) returns (Order);
  rpc WatchOrders (Filter) returns (stream Order);
}
message Order { string id = 1; int64 amount_paise = 2; reserved 3; }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• No deadline, so a slow dependency accumulates threads.
  • Reusing a field number after deleting a field.
  • Debugging as if it were text: use grpcurl and reflection.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are trailers a problem for browsers? -> fetch/XHR do not expose HTTP/2 trailers; gRPC-Web encodes status into the body.
  2. How does a deadline propagate? -> Client sets grpc-timeout; server frameworks derive child call deadlines from the remaining time.
  3. What about gRPC on a public API? -> Usually REST/JSON at the edge with gRPC-JSON transcoding.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "fast binary RPC". Senior explains streams, trailers, deadline propagation, and why gRPC-Web exists.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mobile team could not hit a gRPC backend from the web app until Envoy gRPC-Web was added; the missing Access-Control-Expose-Headers for grpc-status then hid errors from the UI.

questions.contextHtml:
A trading-alerts service uses WebSockets behind nginx. Users on desktop report the feed "freezes" and the app reconnects roughly once a minute, but only when the market is quiet. Server logs show nothing. Config:

location /ws/ {
    proxy_pass http://ws_backend;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
}

Browser console: WebSocket closed: code=1006 at 60-second intervals. nginx error log: upstream timed out (110: Connection timed out) while reading upstream. The app sends no heartbeats; during busy hours it works fine. A colleague blames the CDN in front.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bug(s) and fix them without redeploying clients.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the timeout" without noticing HTTP/1.0 proxying, or blames the CDN/Wi-Fi. It misses that quiet periods are the trigger.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the 60 s exact (suggests a default timeout)? Does it happen only when idle? Any LB or CDN in front with its own idle timeout? Do clients ping?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Raise proxy_read_timeout to 3600s on /ws/ and reload nginx.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: nginx proxy_read_timeout default 60 s; missing proxy_http_version 1.1 (nginx defaults to 1.0 upstream, the upgrade is not forwarded properly); CDN/ALB idle timeout; client NAT expiry.
  4. How I'd verify each: grep 'timed out' error.log and check the 60 s cadence; nginx -T | grep -A8 /ws/; curl -i -N -H 'Upgrade: websocket' -H 'Connection: Upgrade' -H 'Sec-WebSocket-Key: x' -H 'Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13' https://host/ws/ expecting 101; check the ALB attribute idle_timeout.timeout_seconds.
  5. Root cause: nginx closes a connection if the upstream is silent for 60 s. With no ping/pong, quiet markets mean silence, so the proxy cuts it.
  6. Fix: short-term timeout plus proxy_http_version 1.1; long-term server-side ping every 25 s (below every idle timeout in the path), client pong handling, reconnect with jittered backoff.
location /ws/ {
    proxy_pass http://ws_backend;
    proxy_http_version 1.1;
    proxy_set_header Upgrade $http_upgrade;
    proxy_set_header Connection "upgrade";
    proxy_read_timeout 3600s;
}
  1. Prevention: a synthetic WebSocket probe that stays idle for 5 minutes; list of all idle timeouts in the path in the runbook.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not set an infinite timeout (leaked dead peers pin fds); heartbeats are the real fix.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Heartbeat is on but disconnects continue at 350 s? -> NAT gateway idle state expiry (AWS NAT 350 s); ping interval must be well under that.
  • Pings from the server never reach a sleeping mobile client? -> OS suspends sockets; use push notification to wake and reconnect.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team spent two days blaming a CDN for 60 s drops. One grep of the nginx error log showed the exact 60 s cadence; the default timeout had been the culprit since launch, masked by busy-hour traffic.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames network, increases client retries.
  • Hire: finds proxy_read_timeout and proxy_http_version.
  • Strong hire: adds heartbeats under every idle timeout, jittered reconnect, and an idle synthetic probe.

questions.contextHtml:
A live-score page uses SSE. In staging, events arrive instantly. In production, behind nginx and a gzip-enabled CDN rule, viewers see nothing for 20 to 30 seconds, then a burst of 5 to 6 events at once. Direct to the app:

$ curl -N -s https://origin.score.example/stream
id: 811
data: {"over":14.2}
id: 812
data: {"over":14.3}

prints each event the moment it is produced. Through the public hostname the same command prints nothing for ~25 s. App CPU is 8%. A teammate suggests moving to WebSocket.
questions.promptHtml: What is happening and how do you fix it without changing protocol?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Rewrite as WebSocket" or "the app is slow". It ignores that the origin is fast and the problem appears only through proxies.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What sits between the app and user (nginx, CDN, WAF)? Is gzip on for text/event-stream? Does the burst size match a buffer size?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add X-Accel-Buffering: no on the response and bypass the CDN cache/compression for /stream.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: nginx proxy_buffering on; gzip waiting for a full block; CDN buffering responses; app not flushing (ruled out by direct curl).
  4. How I'd verify each: compare curl -N at each hop (app, nginx, CDN edge); curl -sI ... | grep -i content-encoding; nginx -T | grep -E 'buffering|gzip'.
  5. Root cause: nginx collects upstream bytes into 4-8 KB buffers before sending, and gzip adds its own block buffering; 300-byte events take many seconds to fill them.
  6. Fix: proxy_buffering off; (or the header) and gzip off; for the location; set Cache-Control: no-cache; proxy_read_timeout 1h; send : ping comments every 15 s. On the CDN, enable streaming/disable response buffering for the path.
  7. Prevention: a canary that measures event delivery lag end to end (server timestamp vs client receipt) and alerts above 2 s.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not swapping protocols; WebSocket would hit the same idle-timeout issues and lose Last-Event-ID resume.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The CDN cannot stream? -> Serve SSE from a dedicated hostname that bypasses it, or use a CDN with streaming support.
  • 2M viewers? -> Edge fan-out: one origin stream per region, edge relays to viewers.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch-day scoreboard looked 25 s behind for an hour. The compression rule had been applied to every text/* type; excluding text/event-stream fixed it in one line.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: proposes protocol change.
  • Hire: identifies proxy buffering and verifies per hop with curl -N.
  • Strong hire: also handles gzip, keep-alive pings, and measures end-to-end lag.

questions.contextHtml:
Checkout API on Node.js behind an AWS ALB. After a recent upgrade, ALB shows HTTPCode_ELB_502_Count at about 0.15% of requests (300/hour at 55 rps average), no pattern by URL. App logs show no errors for those requests. ALB idle timeout is 60 s. ALB access log lines:

http 2026-11-03T10:14:07 ... 10.0.3.21:8080 -1 -1 -1 502 - ... target_status_code=-

request_processing_time=0.000 target_processing_time=-1. ss -tn state established '( sport = :8080 )' | wc -l is stable at 180. Node server.keepAliveTimeout is default 5 s. CPU is 30%, memory fine. A teammate wants to increase pod count.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale out" or "check app errors"; misses target_processing_time=-1 meaning the target never answered.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Are 502s clustered after quiet periods? Are they on reused connections? Is there an app-level error log for them? What changed in the upgrade (Node version changes keepAlive defaults)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: ALB cannot retry per request, so raise the app keep-alive above 60 s right away (config change plus rolling restart).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: keep-alive timeout mismatch (app closes before ALB idle limit); app crash/OOM restart; target deregistration delay too short; health check flapping.
  4. How I'd verify each: tcpdump -nn -i eth0 'tcp port 8080 and (tcp[tcpflags] & (tcp-fin|tcp-rst) != 0)' showing the app sending FIN after 5 s idle, followed by the ALB's request and an RST; check restarts with kubectl get pods; ALB TargetConnectionErrorCount.
  5. Root cause: the app closes idle connections at 5 s while the ALB keeps them pooled for up to 60 s. When the ALB reuses a connection at the instant the app's FIN is in flight, the request lands on a closed socket and the ALB returns 502.
  6. Fix: set app keep-alive to a value larger than the ALB idle timeout.
server.keepAliveTimeout = 65000;   // > ALB 60 s
server.headersTimeout   = 66000;   // must exceed keepAliveTimeout
  1. Prevention: a standard in the service template: app keep-alive = LB idle + 5 s; alert on HTTPCode_ELB_502_Count / requests above 0.01%.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not scaling pods (does not touch the race) and not lowering the ALB idle timeout below the app's; longer keep-alive uses a little more memory per idle connection.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Same symptoms with nginx as the LB? -> Upstream keepalive_timeout must exceed nginx's idle limit, or nginx marks the upstream failed (proxy_next_upstream).
  • Can retries hide it? -> Retrying only idempotent requests on connection-reset-before-send is safe; blind POST retry can double-charge.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A payments gateway saw random 502s for months; the team added capacity twice. A one-line keep-alive change ended it, and ss showed the pod had 40k short-lived idle sockets all along.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales out or restarts pods.
  • Hire: explains keep-alive mismatch and sets app timeout above LB's.
  • Strong hire: shows evidence with tcpdump, mentions headersTimeout, and a template-level standard.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer, and when do you pick each?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Every system design touches an LB; the signal is knowing what each can and cannot see and the cost of that.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An L4 balancer sees IPs and ports and forwards TCP/UDP bytes; it is very fast, holds millions of connections, and cannot see HTTP. An L7 balancer parses the protocol, so it can route by host, path or header, terminate TLS, retry, rate-limit and cache, at higher CPU cost. I use L4 at the edge for raw throughput or non-HTTP protocols, and L7 where routing, retries or gRPC balancing matter.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
L4 (NLB, LVS/IPVS, Katran): pick backend per CONNECTION (5-tuple hash), copy bytes.
L7 (ALB, Envoy, NGINX):     terminate client conn, pick backend per REQUEST, new/pooled upstream conn.

L7 gains: path routing, per-request balancing (least-request, power-of-two-choices), retries on safe failures, HTTP/2 to clients and HTTP/1.1 upstream, header rewriting, X-Forwarded-For. L4 gains: preserves client IP (or via PROXY protocol), DSR for asymmetric traffic like video, tens of Gbit/s per node. Layering is common: L4 anycast in front of an L7 Envoy fleet.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• L4 in front of gRPC: all calls on one HTTP/2 connection go to one backend.
  • Mismatched timeouts across layers causing random 502/504.
  • Forgetting the LB itself is a SPOF.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How does the app learn the real client IP? -> X-Forwarded-For at L7, PROXY protocol or DSR/transparent at L4.
  2. What is DSR? -> LB rewrites only inbound packets; backend replies directly to the client.
  3. Which algorithm for uneven request cost? -> Least-request with power of two choices, not round robin.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "L7 is smarter". Senior ties choice to per-connection vs per-request balancing, long-lived connections, TLS cost and failure semantics.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A streaming service moved from an L7 to an L4 balancer for ingest and cut LB cost by 70%, then had to add PROXY protocol to keep client IPs for rate limiting.

questions.contextHtml: Product asks for "live" features in a brokerage app: (a) price ticks for a watchlist, 50 symbols per user, 3 updates/s each, 400k concurrent users at peak; (b) order status updates (a few per order); (c) a chat with the support agent; (d) internal services (order, risk, ledger) calling each other at 25k rps. Mobile and web clients. The PM says "just use WebSockets everywhere, it's real time".
questions.promptHtml: What protocol do you choose for each, and what do you ask before deciding?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: One protocol for everything, or a pick without numbers. Misses the mobile background-socket limit and fan-out arithmetic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What latency is acceptable for ticks (100 ms vs 1 s)? Can ticks be conflated (latest per symbol per 250 ms)? Is the web client browser-only? Delivery guarantees on order status? Compliance on message retention?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A (design). I would start with the cheapest path that meets each need.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) SSE or WebSocket with server-side conflation behind an edge fan-out layer; (b) SSE or push notification plus REST fetch of truth; (c) WebSocket (two-way, low latency); (d) gRPC with deadlines.
  4. How I'd verify each: Fan-out math: ticks raw = 400k x 150 msg/s = 60M msg/s, impossible; conflate to 4 updates/s per user sends 1.6M msg/s x ~100 B = 160 MB/s, still needing edge fan-out. Load-test 50k connections per node and measure RAM per socket.
  5. Root cause: N/A. The decision driver is direction, fan-out and client constraints, not buzzwords.
  6. Fix (design): Ticks: SSE (one-way, resume with Last-Event-ID) from edge nodes fed by a pub/sub topic; REST POST for placing orders; order status over the same SSE with push notification when the app is backgrounded; chat on WebSocket; internal calls on gRPC with 300 ms deadlines.
  7. Prevention: A decision record with connection budgets, drain policy, and fallbacks (long polling) if proxies block streaming.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not WebSocket everywhere: it makes every feature stateful and needs custom resume logic. Not raw ticks to mobile: battery and bandwidth.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Ticks must be under 50 ms for pro traders? -> WebSocket with binary frames, region edge nodes, dedicated feed.
  • Corporate proxies break streaming? -> Fall back to long polling behind the same API.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A broker shipped raw ticks over WebSocket to phones; battery drain drove one-star reviews. Conflating to 4 Hz and moving to SSE for read-only data halved traffic and drain.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: one protocol for all, no numbers.
  • Hire: maps each need to a fitting protocol with reasons.
  • Strong hire: does the fan-out arithmetic, conflation, mobile limits and fallback.

questions.promptHtml: Your WebSocket service is stateful. How do you scale it across 20 servers, deliver a message to user B who is connected somewhere else, and survive deploys?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests distributed-systems thinking about connection state, fan-out, and reconnect storms rather than API knowledge.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Connections pin to one node, so I keep a presence map (user to node) in Redis and use pub/sub or a stream to route a message to the right node, which writes to the local socket. Delivery is at-least-once with message ids and acks; clients resume with a last-seen id. Deploys drain gracefully and clients reconnect with jittered backoff to avoid a thundering herd.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Client A -> WS node 1 -> publish(chan:user:B) -> Redis/Kafka
Redis/Kafka -> WS node 7 (subscribed because B connected there) -> Client B

Capacity: ~30 KB per connection, so an 8 GB node holds about 250k sockets if ulimit -n, somaxconn, conntrack and LB-side ephemeral ports allow it. For 5M users online that is about 20 nodes plus headroom. Routing options: broker fan-out by user topic (simple), or consistent hashing by user id to a gateway node (fewer broker hops, rebalances on scale events). Resume: client sends last_id; server replays from a per-user log with a short retention. Backpressure: bounded send queue per socket, drop slow consumers rather than buffer unbounded memory.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Round-robin after a restart leaves uneven counts (first healthy node gets all reconnects). Use least-connections plus connection caps.
  • Presence entries without TTLs go stale after a crash.
  • Assuming no message loss.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you avoid a reconnect storm after deploy? -> Rolling drain with 1001 going away, connection rate limit, client backoff with jitter (0 to 30 s).
  2. How do you handle a slow client? -> Bounded per-socket queue, close with 1013, client resyncs from last id.
  3. How would you shard at 50M connections? -> Cells/regions, per-cell brokers, consistent hash of user id to cell.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "Redis pub/sub". Senior sizes connections per node, defines delivery semantics (at-least-once, ids), presence TTLs, backpressure and deploy drain.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A rolling restart of 12 nodes made 3M clients reconnect in 40 s; the first nodes hit the CPU limit during TLS handshakes. Adding jitter and a handshake rate limiter flattened it.

questions.contextHtml:
Pricing service (gRPC, 6 pods) behind a Kubernetes ClusterIP Service. After adding 6 more pods for a sale, p99 latency stays at 900 ms and one pod is at 95% CPU while others sit at 8%. Metrics per pod:

pod   rps   cpu
p-0   4120  95%
p-1     60   6%
p-2     55   5%
p-3      0   0%   (new)
p-4      0   0%   (new)
...

On the client (order-service, 3 pods) ss -tn dst 10.96.14.22:50051 shows exactly 1 ESTABLISHED connection per client pod. The Service uses kube-proxy iptables mode. A teammate suspects a noisy neighbor and wants to add a bigger node.
questions.promptHtml: Why did adding pods not help, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Bad pod, restart it" or vertical scaling. Does not connect one HTTP/2 connection to L4 balancing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the Service headless or ClusterIP? Is a mesh sidecar present? Do clients create one channel or a pool? How long-lived are connections (max age)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Rolling-restart the clients so they reconnect and spread, as a stopgap, and set MAX_CONNECTION_AGE on servers.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: L4 balancing pinning long-lived HTTP/2 connections; client channel with a single subchannel; slow pod hardware (ruled out by CPU on other nodes); hot key.
  4. How I'd verify each: ss -tn on clients showing 1 connection each; kubectl get endpoints pricing; per-pod rps from Prometheus; grpcurl health on the hot pod; Envoy/Linkerd stats if present.
  5. Root cause: kube-proxy balances per TCP connection. gRPC multiplexes all calls over one HTTP/2 connection, so every call from a client pod lands on whichever backend was picked at connect time. New pods never get connections.
  6. Fix: short-term: server max_connection_age (for example 5 min with grace) so clients reconnect and re-pick. Long-term: client-side load balancing with a headless Service (dns:///pricing-headless:50051, round_robin policy) or an L7 proxy/mesh with per-request balancing.
# client service config
{"loadBalancingConfig":[{"round_robin":{}}]}
  1. Prevention: per-backend rps skew alert (max/min > 3x); load test with more than one backend; scaling runbook "did connections rebalance?".
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not vertical scaling. Connection aging adds brief reconnect cost; client-side LB needs DNS refresh (GRPC_ARG_DNS_RESOLVER re-resolve interval) or xDS.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Headless DNS but new pods still unused? -> Resolver caches; clients only re-resolve on connection failure; enable periodic re-resolution or xDS.
  • Streaming RPCs of 1 hour? -> Aging does not rebalance them; use per-stream rebalancing at deploy or cap stream lifetime.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A sale-day autoscale tripled pods and changed nothing; the dashboard looked like a hot node. Connection count per client was one. Switching to headless round-robin dropped p99 from 900 to 70 ms.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: restarts or upsizes the hot pod.
  • Hire: identifies L4 pinning with HTTP/2 and proposes client-side or L7 balancing.
  • Strong hire: adds connection aging, resolver refresh, skew alert and streaming caveat.

questions.contextHtml:
Edge Envoy retries upstream failures (retry_on: 5xx,reset,connect-failure, num_retries: 3) and clients also retry 3 times. Inventory API normally 2k rps, 40 ms p50. Black Friday traffic goes to 20k rps; a DB failover causes inventory to return 503 for 6 seconds. Envoy stats:

cluster.inventory.upstream_rq_total: 138402
cluster.inventory.upstream_rq_retry: 96311
cluster.inventory.upstream_rq_pending_overflow: 18770

After the DB recovers, the API stays overloaded for 14 minutes (CPU 100%, latency 12 s). The DB is healthy. Queue depth grows then decays slowly.
questions.promptHtml: Why did a 6 s blip become a 14 minute outage, and what do you change before next sale?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more pods". Misses retry amplification (up to 4 x 4 = 16x) and metastable failure.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Retry budgets at each layer? Are POSTs included? Do we have a circuit breaker or outlier detection? Per-request timeouts vs the client timeout?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Shed load: drop retries to 0 at Envoy, enable rate limiting or return 503 with Retry-After at the edge, temporarily scale out.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: retry amplification across layers; timeouts shorter than the work causing duplicated work; no backoff; connection queue overflow (pending_overflow).
  4. How I'd verify each: retry ratio upstream_rq_retry/upstream_rq_total = 70%; request logs correlating client request id counts; ss -s for SYN backlog; app thread pool saturation.
  5. Root cause: each failed request multiplied into up to 16 attempts (3 client retries x 3 Envoy retries plus originals). Load stayed above capacity even after the DB recovered, so queues never drained: a metastable failure.
  6. Fix: short-term: retries off in one layer. Long-term: retry only at one layer; retry budget (for example retries <= 20% of active requests: retry_budget), exponential backoff with jitter, retry_on limited to connect-failure,refused-stream for non-idempotent routes, circuit breaker/outlier ejection, load shedding at the app (fail fast when queue > N), deadlines that shrink per hop.
retry_policy: { retry_on: "connect-failure,refused-stream", num_retries: 1 }
circuit_breakers: { thresholds: [{ max_pending_requests: 200, retry_budget: { budget_percent: { value: 20 } } }] }
  1. Prevention: game-day that kills the DB for 10 s at 10x load; alert on retry ratio > 10%.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not removing retries entirely (transient errors are real); not retrying POST without an idempotency key.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Client library retries are outside our control (mobile apps)? -> Edge rate limit with Retry-After honored via server hints; shed at LB.
  • How do you size the budget? -> Observe steady-state retry rate (about 1%), budget at 10-20%.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A 5 s upstream blip turned into a 20 minute incident across three layers each configured with 3 retries; the post-incident rule became "one retrying layer per call path, with a budget".

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scales out only.
  • Hire: names retry amplification and sets one retry layer with backoff.
  • Strong hire: retry budgets, load shedding, circuit breaking, idempotency and a game-day.

questions.contextHtml:
You are migrating a WebSocket gateway (1.2M concurrent connections on 8 nodes) from nginx to Envoy and from one Kubernetes cluster to another, with zero visible downtime. Each client auto-reconnects on close with a fixed 1 s delay (cannot be changed quickly, mobile release takes weeks). Past deploy: 8 nodes restarted in sequence, and the first node took 400k reconnects in 20 s:

node-1 CPU 100% for 90 s
handshakes/s: 21,500 (limit about 6,000)
`SSL_do_handshake` queue growing; accept queue Recv-Q 4096/4096
nstat: TcpExtListenOverflows 188204

Target: no more than 5% of users see a disconnect longer than 10 s.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch DNS at midnight". Ignores the fixed 1 s reconnect and handshake capacity.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can the server tell clients when to reconnect (a close frame with a reason)? Is there a version header from clients? Are sessions resumable (last id)? What handshake rate can one node do (TLS CPU)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A before migration; first, add server-driven pacing since I cannot change clients: close connections gradually with code 1001 and rely on LB connection rate limits to spread reconnects.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: handshake CPU is the bottleneck; accept queue overflow; sticky first-healthy-node bias in the LB; cold caches on new nodes.
  4. How I'd verify each: load-test new cluster with a synthetic reconnecting fleet (k6/own tool) at 6k handshakes/s; watch ListenOverflows, handshake latency; confirm LB algorithm is least-connections.
  5. Root cause: a fixed 1 s retry synchronizes clients; capacity of a node is bounded by TLS handshakes/s, not steady-state sockets.
  6. Fix (plan): (a) run new gateway in parallel, weighted DNS or LB weights 1% -> 5% -> 25% -> 100%; (b) drain old nodes by closing N connections per second (for example 2,000/s) with 1001, so total reconnect rate stays below new capacity; (c) enable TLS session resumption/tickets to make reconnects cheaper; (d) pre-scale new nodes 2x; (e) rate-limit accepts per node and return a close with reason try-later where clients support it; (f) ship a client update adding jittered exponential backoff.
  7. Prevention: capacity rule: reconnect-rate capacity >= fleet size / target recovery window (1.2M / 120 s = 10k handshakes/s); synthetic probe measuring reconnect time.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a hard DNS cutover; it forces every client to reconnect at once. The drain takes hours but is safe.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Old clients ignore close reason? -> Rate-limit accepts at the LB; clients see refused and retry at 1 s which still spreads them.
  • Region failover? -> Same math: pre-warmed capacity and weighted failover.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A gateway drained 100% in a minute and took itself out with its own reconnects; the re-run drained 2,000 connections per second over 11 minutes and nobody noticed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: DNS flip with an apology banner.
  • Hire: weighted cutover and gradual drain.
  • Strong hire: handshake-rate arithmetic, session tickets, server-side pacing, client backoff release.

questions.contextHtml:
Internal calls between order, pricing and inventory services run as JSON over HTTP/1.1, 20,000 calls/s, average payload 1 KB JSON. The platform lead proposes migrating all 40 services to gRPC "to cut latency". Profiling of order-service:

CPU flame graph: jackson serialization 18%, GC 11%, TLS 9%, handler logic 40%
p50 end-to-end: 38 ms; of which downstream network + parse about 3 ms
New connection per call: 34% of calls (no keepalive pool)

Cloud inter-AZ egress is $0.01/GB each way. Team size 6.
questions.promptHtml: Is the gRPC migration the right first step? What would you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, gRPC is faster" or "no, REST is fine" without numbers or noticing the connection churn.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the goal: latency, cost, or contracts? What share of latency is serialization? Do all languages in the fleet have mature gRPC? Who debugs it on call?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the cheap thing first: enable HTTP keep-alive/pooling (34% of calls pay TCP+TLS handshake).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: connection churn dominates latency tail; serialization is 18% CPU (real but not latency-dominant); payload size matters for egress cost only if cross-AZ.
  4. How I'd verify each: ss -s timewait counts; curl -w timing from a pod; measure bytes: 1 KB JSON vs ~350 B protobuf = 20 MB/s vs 7 MB/s; inter-AZ cost: 13 MB/s saved x 86,400 s ~ 1.1 TB/day ~ $11/day each way.
  5. Root cause: latency is not primarily the wire format; the big avoidable waste is connection setup and logic. gRPC would save maybe 10% CPU and $10-20/day.
  6. Fix: step 1 pooling and HTTP/2 over the existing stack (a day, big win); step 2 pick the 3-4 hottest paths for gRPC where contracts and streaming help; step 3 keep JSON where humans debug and where external partners call; add deadlines everywhere either way.
  7. Prevention: a migration criteria doc: move a service when serialization > 15% CPU or payload > 5 KB at high rps.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a 40-service big bang: tooling (proto registry, L7 balancing, grpc-web) is a real cost. Giving up easy curl debugging is a cost; mitigate with reflection and grpcurl.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Polyglot services in Ruby/PHP? -> Weaker gRPC support; keep REST there.
  • Need streaming for price updates? -> Strong case for gRPC streaming on that path only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A company planned a year-long protobuf migration to save latency; a keep-alive pool config fixed 80% of the tail in an afternoon, and gRPC was then adopted only where streaming helped.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: yes or no without data.
  • Hire: spots connection churn, quantifies savings.
  • Strong hire: stages the migration by measured payoff, calls out L7 balancing and debugging cost.
